headline: AI is moving closer to the experiment: millions of compounds, new enzyme systems, and reusable research workflows are all in view.
summary_for_scientists: This week’s strongest science signal is concrete chemistry and biology work rather than generic AI claims. A model scanned 4.6 million compounds for hydrogen-position predictions, while a Claude-assisted workflow surfaced a previously unknown enzyme system. The practical thread is reproducibility: connect the model to a familiar dataset and keep the path from input to result visible.

lab_pick.title: AI scans 4.6 million compounds to predict hydrogen positions
lab_pick.what_they_did: Researchers trained an AI model to learn chemical patterns associated with stability and predict where hydrogen atoms should be positioned across a large compound set.
lab_pick.result: The work covered 4.6 million compounds and showed how a model can make a high-volume chemistry search tractable.
lab_pick.why_researchers_care: It is close to a real materials or chemistry question: reduce a huge candidate space to a set a scientist can investigate next.
lab_pick.how_to_share: Demo the paper in a lab meeting with a familiar compound family, then ask the team which small prediction they would want to reproduce first.
